overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing One Chapter, Opening Another
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 13a–13b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes reconciling when a firstborn donkey must be redeemed, then closes the first chapter with a mishna listing several pairs of mitzvot where one option takes precedence over another. A new mishna opens the second chapter with the same five gentile-partnership scenarios as before — now applied to a cow's fetus, whose sanctity is inherent rather than merely monetary — prompting the Gemara to ask why the donkey was taught first at all. The daf closes with an extended discussion of how a Jew acquires property from a gentile, tested against the tricky case of an idol discovered inside purchased scrap metal.

slides.title: ⏰ Reconciling 'Immediately' and 'After Thirty Days' — Round Two
slides.subtitle: A contradiction between baraitot, resolved twice over

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Sheshet: 'immediate' means one may redeem right away and it's valid; 'after thirty days' means only then does failing to redeem become an active transgression

2️⃣ Rami bar Ḥama objects: a baraita says 'the mitzva applies throughout the thirty days; from then on, EITHER redeem it OR break its neck' — doesn't this mean the ideal is to wait the full thirty days?
3️⃣ Reinterpreted: no, it means there is a mitzva to redeem it at any point during the thirty days, and only afterward does failing to redeem become a transgression

4️⃣ Rava's cleaner resolution: the two baraitot are simply two opinions — Rabbi Eliezer compares donkey-redemption to a firstborn SON's (wait until 30 days); the Rabbis reject that comparison and require immediate redemption

slides.title: 📜 When One Mitzva Takes Precedence — Closing the First Chapter
slides.subtitle: A mishna listing which of two options comes first
rows: Redeeming a firstborn donkey vs. breaking its neck
Redemption first — 'if you will not redeem it, THEN you shall break its neck' (Exodus 13:13)
Designating a Hebrew maidservant vs. redeeming her with money
Designation first — 'who has not betrothed her...then he shall let her be redeemed' (Exodus 21:8)
Originally yibum first (Deuteronomy 25:7) — but once performed without pure motive, the Sages reversed it: ḥalitza now comes first
An owner redeeming his own consecrated non-kosher animal vs. anyone else redeeming it
The owner first — 'and if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold' (Leviticus 27:27) implies he gets first opportunity

slides.title: 🐄 Why Donkey Before Cow?
slides.subtitle: A new mishna opens chapter two with the same structure, now for a cow

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The new mishna repeats the same five gentile-partnership cases, now for a cow's fetus (inherent sanctity, offered on the altar) instead of a donkey's (mere value-sanctity). Shouldn't the more significant case have been taught first?

lines.speaker: Answer 1
lines.text: Donkeys are dear to the tanna — recall Rabbi Ḥanina's teaching that donkeys assisted Israel at the Exodus, carrying Egypt's silver and gold.

lines.speaker: Answer 2
lines.text: Or: the laws of a non-kosher animal are relatively few, so the tanna completes that smaller topic before moving to the larger one.

lines.speaker: New ruling
lines.text: The new mishna also adds: priests and Levites are obligated for a firstborn kosher animal — unlike their exemption from a firstborn son or firstborn donkey.

slides.title: 💰 Acquiring an Animal From a Gentile: Money Alone Suffices
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish's ruling, in the name of Rabbi Oshaya

nodes.content: ❓ A Jew who pays a gentile for an animal 'according to their laws' — is the sale complete with MONEY ALONE, without pulling? This decides whether the firstborn offspring is obligated or exempt.
🤔 First guess: like acquiring a gentile SLAVE, where money alone works — rejected, since even between two Jews, a slave's body is bought with money but PROPERTY still needs pulling
✅ Abaye's source: 'buy of your counterpart's hand' (Leviticus 25:14) — from a fellow Jew you need PULLING; by implication, from a gentile's hand, money ALONE suffices
🔄 The reverse holds too: a gentile who pays a Jew for an animal likewise acquires it with money alone, exempting its firstborn

slides.title: 🗿 The Idol Test Case: Four Ways to Read One Baraita
slides.subtitle: Scrap metal from gentiles conceals an idol — when was it acquired?

boxes.title: Abaye
items: Pulled before paying (returnable): a genuine mistaken sale — the buyer never wanted an idol
Pulled after paying (must discard): not mistaken — he should have inspected before pulling once he'd already paid

boxes.title: Rava
items: The real difference is optics: before payment, an idol doesn't yet 'look like' it's the Jew's; after payment, it does

boxes.title: Rav Ashi / Ravina
items: Disagree about which clause is the anomaly
Rav Ashi: neither clause shows pulling as effective
Ravina: both do — the first clause is reread as merely retracting a verbal promise

summary.principle: The first chapter closes by ranking competing mitzvot and fixing when a firstborn donkey must be redeemed; the second opens with the parallel case of a firstborn cow and a close look at how a Jew acquires property — including a live animal — from a gentile.

flowSteps.content: ⏰ Redemption is valid immediately, though Rabbi Eliezer holds the ideal timing (like a firstborn son) is after thirty days
📜 The chapter closes by ranking several pairs of competing mitzvot, redemption over neck-breaking among them

columns.content: 🐄 Chapter two opens with the same gentile-partnership rules, now for a cow's inherently sanctified firstborn
💰 A Jew acquires an animal from a gentile with money alone, tested against a tricky idol-in-scrap-metal case

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: acquisition from a gentile follows its own rule — money alone, mirroring how the Torah singles out acquisition 'from your counterpart' as requiring pulling

quiz.q: According to Rava's resolution of the 'immediately' vs. 'after thirty days' contradiction, whose opinion requires waiting until the donkey is thirty days old, and why?
o: The Rabbis, because they compare it to consecrated property
Rabbi Eliezer, because he compares redeeming a firstborn donkey to redeeming a firstborn son, which occurs after thirty days
Rabbi Yehuda, because of the prohibition on deriving benefit
No one requires waiting; it is always immediate
quiz.e: Rava explains that the baraita requiring a thirty-day wait follows Rabbi Eliezer, who compares the donkey's redemption to a firstborn son's (Numbers 18:16); the Rabbis reject this comparison and require immediate redemption.

quiz.q: According to the mishna closing the first chapter, which takes precedence: redeeming a firstborn donkey or breaking its neck?
o: Breaking its neck always comes first
Redemption takes precedence, derived from 'if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck'
They are performed simultaneously
It depends on the owner's preference alone, with no textual basis
quiz.e: The mishna derives from Exodus 13:13's wording — redemption named before neck-breaking — that redemption is the preferred, primary option.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna opening the second chapter, are priests and Levites obligated in the firstborn status of a kosher animal such as a cow?
o: No, they are exempt just as with a firstborn donkey
Yes — unlike their exemption from a firstborn son or firstborn donkey, they are fully obligated for a kosher animal's firstborn
Only Levites are obligated, not priests
The mishna does not address this question
quiz.e: The mishna explicitly states that priests and Levites were exempted only from redeeming a firstborn son and a firstborn donkey, but remain obligated regarding a firstborn kosher animal.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, from what verse is it derived that a Jew can acquire an animal from a gentile through payment of money alone, without pulling?
o: 'I sanctified to Me all the firstborn' (Numbers 3:13)
'Buy of your counterpart's hand' (Leviticus 25:14) — implying pulling is needed specifically from a fellow Jew, while money alone suffices from a gentile
'And you shall redeem the firstborn of a donkey with a lamb' (Exodus 13:13)
There is no verse; it is a purely rabbinic enactment
quiz.e: Abaye reads 'of your counterpart's hand' as limiting the requirement of pulling to transactions between Jews, implying that money alone completes an acquisition from a gentile.

quiz.q: According to Rava's explanation of the idol-in-scrap-metal baraita, what is the key difference between pulling the idol before versus after paying for it?
o: There is no real difference; the rulings are identical
It is a matter of appearances — before payment, the idol doesn't yet look like it belongs to the Jew; after payment, it does
Pulling before payment is always invalid under Jewish law
The difference concerns only the idol's monetary value
quiz.e: Rava explains both clauses involve a mistaken transaction, but the practical ruling differs based on how it appears to onlookers: after payment, the idol appears to be in the Jew's possession and so cannot simply be returned.
